stories.headline: Israeli strike on Gaza's Nasser hospital kills six Palestinians, health ministry says
stories.summary:
An Israeli air strike on Nasser hospital, the largest medical facility in the southern Gaza Strip, killed at least six people and injured about 20 overnight, according to the Hamas-run health ministry. Eyewitnesses told the BBC that a single missile fired from a warplane struck a five-storey building housing surgical wards and intensive care units. The ministry said medical staff, patients and companions were among the dead, including surgeon Dr Rizk Abu Shaira, and condemned the attack as a "flagrant violation of international laws and conventions."

The Israeli military said it targeted a commander of Hamas's armed wing and other fighters who it said used the hospital as a "headquarters" to plan attacks on Israeli forces. Israel has long accused Hamas of exploiting civilian infrastructure, including hospitals, to store weapons and run command rooms, which Hamas denies. Hamas said Israel was spreading "false narratives" in an attempt to cover up a "new war crime." Israel bars international news organisations from Gaza, so the competing claims could not be independently verified.

Hospitals have protected status under international law but have been repeatedly hit during the war. Nasser hospital was struck twice in August 2025, killing at least 20 people, including journalists and health workers. Israeli strikes have continued despite the ceasefire agreement of October last year, and the health ministry, whose figures the UN considers reliable, says more than 1,620 people have been killed since then. Each side accuses the other of violating the truce.

The strike comes as conditions in Gaza deteriorate further, with heavy rains reportedly flooding tens of thousands of tents sheltering displaced families.

stories.headline: Biden says he would not have sought second term had he known he had cancer
stories.summary:
Former President Joe Biden said he did not know he had cancer while in office and would not have run for a second term had he been diagnosed. In an interview with People magazine ahead of the release of his White House memoir, Biden said, "If I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer, I would've not gone forward." He added that he does not think "an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running" for president.

Biden was diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer months after leaving office in 2025, and his son Hunter said in August that the cancer had spread and was causing pain. Biden, who turns 84 on Nov. 20, defended his record, saying age was not disqualifying and that he was "the best-equipped person to do the job." He downplayed his disastrous June 2024 debate against Donald Trump, saying he expected another debate and did not consider it consequential, though it accelerated Democratic concerns about his age. He ended his campaign within weeks and endorsed Kamala Harris, who lost to Trump.

Biden also defended his pardon of Hunter Biden, saying Trump's "penchant for vengeance" made it necessary and that he pardoned family members and others who had dealt with him to shield them from retaliation. Hunter Biden has said the pardon damaged his father's legacy. Republicans have long argued Biden's age and fitness were concealed from the public, while Biden's allies say he performed his duties capably. The memoir, which also says Trump should carry the weight of the Jan. 6 riots, is due out Tuesday.

stories.headline: Ukrainians endure rolling blackouts as Russia intensifies strikes on power grid
stories.summary:
Ukrainians are facing rolling planned power cuts as intensified Russian attacks batter the country's energy grid, even as US envoys prepare to meet the Russian and Ukrainian leaders on Thursday. The outages began earlier this year than last winter and are already lasting longer. In Kyiv, some families report outages of up to 20 hours a day, and one resident described getting only two hours of electricity followed by eight without.

Officials worry life could become unsustainable for millions of people if supply cannot be maintained for at least four hours a day, and some warn privately that the threshold is close. Kyiv has been hit hardest, with metro trains and trolleybuses at times brought to a standstill, and hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians nationwide have lost power in recent weeks. Without electricity, lifts, water pumps, heating and internet fail, leaving residents in cold, dark apartments as temperatures fall.

The BBC visited one of Ukraine's largest power stations, which it was asked not to name for security reasons, and found it reduced to twisted metal and broken pipes after a recent ballistic missile strike described as the most powerful of Russia's campaign against energy targets. Ukraine has responded by striking Russian oil refineries. The pressure on civilians adds urgency to the diplomatic track, which has included talks in Abu Dhabi and an agreed prisoner exchange.

stories.headline: Driver accused of DUI in Los Angeles crash that killed three pedestrians
stories.summary:
The driver of a minivan that slammed into sidewalk vendors and pedestrians outside the North Hollywood Metro station in Los Angeles was allegedly driving under the influence and has been arrested on murder counts, police said Wednesday. Ihor Demianenko, 61, is accused of crashing into people around 5:55 p.m. Tuesday at Lankershim and Chandler boulevards. Three women between 40 and 60 were killed, and two other women, aged 50 to 55, remain in critical condition.

Police said the impact sent pedestrians and debris flying. Council member Adrin Nazarian said the driver was under the influence of alcohol and veered to the right off the road before striking people on the sidewalk. The LAPD initially said the driver was critically hurt but later said his injuries were minor. His bail was set at more than $6 million, and it was unclear whether he had an attorney.

Mayor Karen Bass said she was heartbroken for the families, while Mayor-elect Nithya Raman, who defeated Bass in last week's election, said the loss of street vendors who had served the community for years was especially devastating. A witness described one of the victims as a fixture of the neighborhood who worked the same corner every day.
